# Baseline report: DRAFT (generated by tools/baseline_draft.py; do not edit by hand)

Every number below is read from the run outputs. Reference path: net replacement S3-10; near-term join `market_excess`.

## Summary

New Zealand is projected to build 89.6 million m² of new residential floor area in 2026-2050 on the reference path, embodying 31.0 Mt CO₂e over the life cycle, of which 21.6 Mt is upfront (materials A1-A5 plus soil). How fast existing dwellings are replaced is the largest structural uncertainty: Low (S1, the long-run rate) gives 83.2 million m², High (S2, the 2018-2023 rate persisting) 98.7 million m² (typology shares held in every scenario). Within the reference path, joint uncertainty in the inputs gives a 90% interval of 69.1-109.9 million m² (median 88.9, mean 89.1). Outside the MC, carbon-factor and soil bounds on the reference carbon (31,013 kt): case-study jackknife 29,845-32,104 kt, single case study 23,873-37,623 kt, soil order 29,358-38,020 kt. Population uncertainty alone (Stats NZ 5th-95th percentiles) spans 66.7-112.3 million m². The joint interval is narrower than the population-only range because each population draw also moves household size along the matching Stats NZ Low/High variant: low-population variants come with smaller households (an older age structure), so the number of households varies less than population, whereas the population-only range holds household size on the Medium shape. Upfront carbon (21.6 Mt) is the quantity comparable with a 2026-2050 budget; the later life-cycle stages are booked in the construction year but emitted mostly after 2050.

### Near-term rule: "near-term market excess"

2026 building is observed, not modelled: 38,863 dwellings = 0.95 x consents over the latest 12 observed months (the year to July 2026; to be replaced by calendar 2026 when published). It exceeds the 2026 requirement by +16,760. From 2027 building stays above the requirement by gap_ref x rho^(t-2026), with gap_ref = building 2026 - requirement 2027 = +9,974 and rho = 0.52 (the estimated persistence of departures from the calibrated identity). The 2027 requirement is used because the 2026 requirement is depressed by the one-off 2026 population shortfall. The excess is STOCK-ADDING: the extra dwellings join the stock as additional vacancy that is not absorbed (no payback), soil applies (new footprints) and removals stay on the scenario path; +27,479 dwellings over 2026-2050, on top of whichever replacement scenario runs. Implied vacancy (1 - households / (stock + excess)) peaks at 6.52% in 2031 and is 6.36% in 2050, against 5.08-8.09% at the censuses 1986-2023 (pre-2013 values on the earlier empty definition).

Implied vacancy stays about 1.0 point above the 2023 rate because the surplus is never absorbed; with payback (absorption 0.20 a year) floor area is -4.1%.

Caveats: a permanent surplus assumes the extra vacancy is never absorbed; over 2018-2023 part of the excess went to redevelopment and household formation instead. rho is estimated on the calibrated identity, not on market cycles. Sensitivities: booking as stock-neutral redevelopment (implied net removals then peak at 23,041 in 2026), payback (absorption 0.20 or 0.10 a year), and the gap measured against the 2026 requirement.

### Soil method

Soil organic carbon loss is land-use change: a new building footprint seals the soil under it, while a rebuilt footprint sits on soil already sealed. Soil loss is therefore applied to all non-replacement floor area and is zero on the replacement bands (demolition replacement, the calibrated residual and the redevelopment channel). The factor is 58.77 kg CO₂e per m² of footprint, the area-weighted average over the 10 soil orders of the land zoned for urbanisation to about 2050 in Auckland, divided by each typology's floor space index (Christoforatos, Pickering & Schipper 2026, Journal of Environmental Management 415, 130603, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.130603). The Raw and Organic soil-order extremes are the bounding sensitivity. Carbon factors for materials come from 16 New Zealand case studies (Christoforatos & Pickering 2025, Smart and Sustainable Built Environment, https://doi.org/10.1108/SASBE-06-2025-0304).

## Validation

Rolling-origin hindcast of dwellings built (actual households and vacancy fed in; the net-replacement term predicted). Vacancy on a consistent definition (the pooled 2018/2023 empty share, 49.2% of unoccupied, at every census; the 2013 census share was 76.2%, and published empty vacancy falls 8.09% -> 5.08% across the 2013->2018 definitional break); vacancy as published in the last column.

| origin | test years | long-run rate (S1) error | reference method (S3-10) error | best alternative | reference, vacancy as published |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2006 | 2007-2023 | -7.1% | -6.1% | constant -0.4% | -16.2% |
| 2013 | 2014-2023 | -4.4% | -2.0% | constant -0.8% | -18.0% |
| 2018 | 2019-2023 | -14.7% | -10.5% | linked -8.5% | -10.5% |

Under a consistent vacancy definition the reference method reproduces building from the 2006 and 2013 origins to 2023 within 2-6%; the residual miss (-10.5% from 2018) is the 2018-23 surge.

2026 check (model run without any observed-2026 input): observed consents Jan-Jul 23,916 vs model 17,389; ratio 1.38.
Decomposition of the 2026 gap on the reference path (Jan-Jul 2026 / seasonal share): +11,049 dwellings = population -6,157 + pipeline from 2025 +0 + 2026 consents above requirement +17,206.

## Finding: 2026 building runs well above the model's requirement

Consents for January-July 2026 (23,916) are 1.38 times what the reference model, run without any 2026 data, implies for those months. In completions, observed-implied 2026 building is 40,482 dwellings against a reference-path requirement of 29,434 (gap +11,049)[^s1]. Population does not explain it: growth over the year to June 2026 fell short of the projection, which lowers the requirement by 6,157. The gap is building already in the pipeline from 2025 (+0) plus 2026 consents above requirement (+17,206). Over 2018-2023 most building above household formation went to redevelopment (net removals 30,207) rather than vacancy (+6,286).

The model takes 2026 building from the observed consents and carries the excess forward as near-term market excess (+16,760 dwellings in 2026, then gap_ref +9,974 fading at rho = 0.52; +27,479 dwellings over 2026-2050).

[^s1]: On S1 (long-run replacement) the requirement is 27,574 and the gap +12,908 = population -6,157 + pipeline +0 + 2026 consents above requirement +19,066.

## Planetary-boundary layer (climate change)

Against the 2 °C carrying capacity (Bjørn & Hauschild 2015), allocated to the sector by acquired rights (AR; Horup et al. 2025) and ability to pay (AtP; Hjalsted et al. 2021), the boundary is 242.2 kt CO2e (AR) and 43.35 kt (AtP) in 2026, and 256.2 / 45.87 kt in 2050 (AtP = 17.9% of AR in every year). Over 2026-2050 the reference path exceeds them 4.99-fold (AR; MC p5-p95 4.00-5.92) and 27.9-fold (AtP; 22.1-33.2). The two principles are a range and are not averaged. Methods, constants, sources and limitations: outputs/PB_METHODS_DRAFT.md; settings: ASSUMPTIONS.md.

## Open limitations and data needs

- No national demolition data: demolition of detached buildings up to three storeys is consent-exempt, so the implied replacement rates cannot be tested against a count.
- N4 (open): the Low/High household-size variants (deterministic) are paired with stochastic population percentiles through one draw z, and the total vs private-household population question is unresolved until the living-arrangement table (E2); the household projections are 2018-base, with Stats NZ's 2023-base release (late 2026) to be adopted in a later version.
- Timber end of life (C1-C4) excludes biogenic CO2 (confirmed by the author). Whether it includes landfill methane is TO CONFIRM from Christoforatos & Pickering 2025 (author check).
- With shares held in every scenario, neither the scenarios nor the Monte Carlo carry typology-mix uncertainty; the mix is treated as a pathway lever (next paper), not as a baseline uncertainty.
- The soil factor was derived for Auckland's future urban zones and is applied nationally.
- Apartments rest on one independent case study (A_1 and A_2 are one design at two scales).
- The regional analysis of the rebuilding wave (replacement half-life by territorial authority) is deferred.
- Net replacement persistence (S3 half-life) is not identifiable from the census record; S1 and S2 bound it.
- The 2018 census empty-dwelling count has no quality rating (DataInfo+); the vacancy terms rely on it.
- The near-term excess fades at the persistence estimated on the calibrated stock identity (rho), not on market cycles (an assumption).
- W from Little's law is a lower bound on the completion lag.
- Retirement-village floor area is reported but out of carbon scope.
- The near-term surplus (≈27,500 dwellings over 2026-2050, of which ≈24,600 in 2026-2028) is not absorbed by later demand; implied vacancy therefore rises from 5.4% (2023 census) to ≈6.4% and remains there, about 1 percentage point above the 1986-2023 range on a consistent definition (4.0-5.4%). Absorption is not modelled: the persistence rho = 0.52 (lag-1 autocorrelation of the annual departure of building from the calibrated stock identity, 1992-2023) describes how a flow deviation fades (already used for the excess), not a payback of the stock, and the eight census vacancy observations do not identify a mean-reversion rate.
- Decarbonisation paths are relative changes for European and global market processes modelled with premise on ecoinvent 3.9.1 (Horup et al. 2025); they are applied as relative changes to New Zealand case-study factors. This assumes NZ material supply decarbonises at the same relative rate as those markets, which is not tested. Items without a counterpart in Horup et al. follow a labelled proxy path (polymers, paint and SIP at EPS, the smallest reduction in the set; gypsum plasterboard at clay brick) or are held at 2025 (the lift); the proxies are a judgement, bracketed by holding them at 2025 (sensitivity).
- B4 (replacement) and C1-C4 (end of life) occur decades after construction but are booked in the construction year and held at 2025 factors; future production and end-of-life technology would lower them (conservative).
- Horup et al. (2025) SI Table S4 gives the average of the 9 premise scenarios only; the scenario range is shown graphically in their Fig. 2, so no low/high decarbonisation path is implemented.
- Several items are made in New Zealand with electricity-intensive production (aluminium, Pink Batts glass wool, Pacific Steel rebar, WPMA Radiata timber, Nelson Pine LVL); the aluminium items are stated in their EPD names to use mainly renewables-generated electricity. Where their 2025 factors already reflect low-carbon electricity, the premise paths, which include the decarbonisation of electricity supply ("The Premise software accounts for future changes in several critical sectors (supply of conventional and alternative fuels, electricity, cement and steel production and freight and passenger road transportation), and includes implementation of technologies such as carbon capture and storage in steel and cement production" (Horup et al. 2025, p. 5)), may overstate their relative reduction; a sensitivity holds them at 2025.
- Composite floor decking (an RC item containing its steel deck and rebar) follows the concrete-structure path because the source gives no split; this is conservative versus steel profile for the steel share.
